rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation removes (float) cast from fabsf((float)val3) → fabsf(val3). Given input dtype=torch.float32, the AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES macro instantiates scalar_t=float. Since val3 is already float, (float)val3 is a no-op cast. Both fabsf((float)val3) and fabsf(val3) compile to identical operations when val3 is float. No value can distinguish them.
rounds.survival_reason: The input specification fixes dtype=torch.float32, which means the CUDA template parameter scalar_t is instantiated as float. The mutation changes fabsf((float)val3) to fabsf(val3), but since val3 is already of type float (from scalar_t val3 = input[idx + 3]), the explicit (float) cast is redundant. In C/C++/CUDA, casting a float to float is a semantic no-op that produces identical machine code. The fabsf function expects a float argument, and passing a float value directly vs casting it first produces bit-identical results. This is confirmed by Layer 2 testing showing bitwise equivalence across 112 rounds including stress tests with various value distributions.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation only affects behavior when scalar_t=double (i.e., torch.float64 input), but the input dtype is fixed as torch.float32. With float inputs, the cast (float)val3 is a no-op.
rounds.recommendations: When mutation testing CUDA kernels with AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES, consider that type-cast mutations may only be killable for specific dtype instantiations. Test coverage should include both float32 and float64 inputs to catch precision-related mutations that affect double but not float paths.
